hook.text: A German company and a Japanese company report profits. Can you compare them? Not easily.

buildup.text: Every country had its own accounting rules, making cross-border investing a nightmare.

discovery.text: In 2001, the IASB was created to develop International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).

twist.text: Over 140 countries now use IFRS. The U.S. still uses GAAP—the biggest holdout.

climax.text: The push for one global accounting language continues, but full convergence remains elusive.

punchline.text: One world, two rule books. The debate goes on.

quiz.question: How many countries currently use IFRS?

details.summary: International Financial Reporting Standards emerged in the late 20th century to create a single global accounting language, allowing investors to compare financial statements from companies in different countries using consistent rules.
details.whyItMatters: IFRS adoption by over 140 countries represents the most significant standardization in accounting history, enabling truly global capital markets and cross-border investment analysis.
takeaways: IFRS was created to provide a single set of accounting standards usable worldwide
Over 140 countries now require or permit IFRS for financial reporting
IFRS uses principles-based standards while U.S. GAAP tends to be more rules-based

faq.question: What is IFRS and why was it created?
faq.answer: Both IFRS and GAAP aim for accurate financial reporting, but IFRS is principles-based (broader guidelines, more judgment) while GAAP is rules-based (specific detailed rules). IFRS is used in over 140 countries; GAAP is primarily used in the United States.

faq.question: How many countries use IFRS?
faq.answer: Over 140 countries now require or permit IFRS for financial reporting by publicly traded companies. The United States remains the largest economy still using its own standard (GAAP), though convergence efforts have aligned many rules between the two systems.
